blocks.text: …the last day her mother was seen. And the child singing on that tape couldn't have been you. You weren't born until 1999."
The elderly woman was named Ruth Abbott. The case was a probate dispute over her late son's estate.

In 1992, Ruth's son, Michael, had a daughter named Grace with a young woman named Linda. The relationship fell apart. In March 1996, Linda, struggling with severe depression, left four-year-old Grace with Michael and disappeared. The tape was a voicemail Linda left on Ruth's answering machine that night, with Grace singing in the background: "Please tell him I'm sorry."

Michael moved away with Grace and cut off contact with his own mother. He died last year, leaving a large estate to "my daughter, Grace." A woman had come forward claiming to be Grace, with documents that looked convincing. Ruth didn't believe her.
Ruth's attorneys had tracked Linda's later life. She'd gotten treatment, recovered, moved to another state, remarried, and had another daughter in 1999. Me.

She'd sung that song to me every night because it was the song she'd made up for her first daughter, the one she'd left behind and never forgave herself for losing. She died when I was twelve. She never told me I had a sister.

The attorneys hadn't brought me in as an audio expert. They'd brought me in because a DNA test from me could prove whether the woman claiming to be Grace was really my mother's daughter. I agreed on the spot.
She wasn't. The woman was an acquaintance of Michael's who'd found his papers.

Then the attorneys used my DNA again, on genealogy databases, and found the real Grace within a month. She was thirty-four, a teacher in Delaware, raised by her father under a different last name. She'd been told her mother abandoned her and never looked back.

I flew to Delaware with a copy of the tape. We sat in her kitchen, and I played it. She went completely still when she heard her four-year-old voice singing. Then she started humming along. She remembered every note.

I told her what our mother was like: funny, sad sometimes, and how every night at bedtime she sang that song to me. "She was singing it to both of us," Grace said quietly. "She just didn't know where I was."
Ruth met her granddaughter for the first time in thirty years that spring. Grace sang her the song.
